📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” indicates the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

Sources indicate that the first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” claims Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”.

In a recent development, but embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman claims. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”.

In a recent development, wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

Sources indicate that first and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

It has been revealed that about five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Recent findings suggest that somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Industry observers note that christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

According to recent reports, it was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

In a recent development, it’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very crucial for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

It has been revealed that then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

Recent findings suggest that and so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Industry observers note that very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”.

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Industry observers note that those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we introduced, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance looks were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we released, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very promptly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We released overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

Industry observers note that it’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

Industry observers note that I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics challenges, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some challenges we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process indicated with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

It has been revealed that then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really demonstrated through when we were out there.

Industry observers note that I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

According to recent reports, we saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

Sources indicate that it’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦.

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

Thankfully, many of these executive orders are being challenged in court. But the messaging has already infiltrated the brains of Trump supporters (and beyond) far and wide, normalizing these hateful thoughts and actions in our country.

It has been revealed that so what do we do? We speak out and spread facts. Especially with those closest to us who might not be informed or might not understand. That’s not always easy though, especially when emotions get involved and you end up getting upset and flustered. To help, I tapped three experts to create a list of responses to common (and problematic) refrains about the trans community you might come across in future discussions.

In any discourse with someone who doesn’t think like you, it’s always important to make sure the other party knows you’re actually also listening—not just arguing. But if tensions do get high, the Q&As below can serve as a script of sorts to fall back on when you want to make sure you’re hitting all the key talking points while supporting and speaking up for the trans community.

What sex is someone who is born without a vagina but has XX chromosomes (MRKH Syndrome)? What sex is someone who has XXY chromosomes and little to no detectable testosterone levels in adulthood (Klinefelter syndrome)?

But let’s take a step back and look at this from a different angle: Gender and sex are different. Gender identity develops long before the physical change of puberty. People generally know their gender long before secondary sex characteristics develop, because gender identity has its own strong biological basis rooted in the brain and it exists separately from chromosomes, gonads, and hormones.

For other people, their inner sense of self is different from their sex assigned at birth, causing an incongruence with who they know themselves to be and how the world sees them. This person might call themselves transgender. That doesn’t make anyone’s gender more or less valid than someone else’s—it just means they’re different. At the end of the day, we don’t expect everyone to know exactly what it means to be transgender, but we do expect people to respect each other, even when we are different.

Here’s the good news: Except for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which came out this summer and is now on digital, every Marvel Cinematic Universe movie is available on Disney+. Every. Single. One.

When Steve Rogers gave Sam Wilson (Anthony Mackie) the shield of Captain America in Endgame, Sam wasn’t ready to take up the responsibility so soon. He still had his own things to work out. After the Disney+ series The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Sam now flies the skies as Captain America, with the 2025 film Captain America: Brave Fresh World marking the start of his era as the Star-Spangled Man. In addition to being the fourth Captain America movie, the movie revisits the events of 2008’s The Incredible Hulk and 2021’s Eternals.

The Marvel franchise was built on a studio elevating comic book benchwarmers into A-listers. That tradition was upheld in the 2025 movie Thunderbolts*. Based on a Marvel Comics series where supervillains form a team, the major-screen version recruits several “forgotten” antiheroes from different corners of the MCU. Together, they form a fresh team that must stave off their own assassination and save the world—on their terms. You can watch the movie cold, but know that many of these characters come from movies like Captain America: The Winter Soldier, Black Widow, Ant-Man and the Wasp, and the TV show The Falcon and the Winter Soldier.

And now, we step into a whole ‘nother world. After multiple attempts at a major-screen Fantastic Four, the Marvel Cinematic Universe debuted its own take on the First Family in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. Set on a different Earth in 1964, the Fantastic Four rise to the occasion when the planet is threatened by Galactus.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026).

Sources indicate that look. Don’t put yourself through that. There are too many. If you insist on watching any of them, just watch Loki. It has two seasons and just 12 episodes total, so you can knock it out in one weekend. Loki takes place after Avengers: Endgame (technically after just The Avengers, but how and why is too long to explain), and of all the shows, it bears the strongest ties to Doomsday. Talk about a glorious purpose.

  • Recent findings suggest that this bomber jacket has some history to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 1957, Canada Goose has been crushing the luxury outerwear game. And if its decades of history tell you one thing, it’s that Canada Goose isn’t going anywhere anytime soon. In fact, one of the best decisions that you can make is investing in a piece or two (if you haven’t already) because it’s a purchase that’s going to pay off. The high-quality designs are durable, practical, and stand at a timeless intersection where fashion meets function.

Industry observers note that the biggest glitch we have with Canada Goose is that there are too many options to choose from. You’re probably already aware that the brand has more than just its hefty parkas. Sure, it’s got those too, of course, but we also love its bombers, flannels, and fleeces. Canada Goose brand has even been venturing into the high-fashion space, with its creative director Haider Ackermann debuting collaborations with the NBA’s Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, CNCPTS, and KidSuper, among others.To help you find the right fit for you, we did a full breakdown for you. Below, find our official guide to the six best Canada Goose jackets. You’re not going to regret getting any of these.

Recent findings suggest that this bomber jacket has some history to it. Originally designed over 25 years ago, this iteration of the jacket fuses modern functionality with classic bomber detailing, like a double placket, pen pocket, and ribbed waist. The archive-inspired satin gives it a glossy finish, but it’s still subtle enough that it will go with pretty much just about anything. Wear it with some black jeans, combat or Chelsea boots, and you’ve got a badass fit.

Every man should own a bomber jacket, so if for some reason the Seguin Aviator didn’t resonate with you, maybe this one will. Inspired by the brand’s 2004 Air Force parka, this bomber adds a warm fleece for insulation—as well as style points. With five pockets (two welt pockets at the chest, two lower pockets with coin-snaps, one zippered sleeve pocket), it masters practicality.

In a recent development, you can never go wrong with a traditional puffer. It’s actually more of a prerequisite than anything else, especially if you live somewhere with an actual winter. Canada Goose’s puffer is top-of-the-line, as it’s ultra-lightweight, super soft, and durable. So many puffer jackets weigh you down, but this one doesn’t. Its features are also endless: There are backpack straps, recessed rib-knit cuffs that add comfort and lock in heat, interior drawcord to customize fit, two exterior fleece-lined handwarmer pockets with zipper closures, three interior pockets, two mesh drop-in pockets, one security pocket—and more.

If you want a streamlined parka that doesn’t have too much going on on the outside—but still has a ton of cool features inside—the Langford is the one for you. It has a sleek silhouette that’s slightly longer than a puffer, and it’s even warmer than a puffer, too. With 625 Fill Power down inside, it can protect you in temperatures down to -13°F, and it will look great while doing it. It also has an adjustable down-filled hood, lined chin guard, two-way zipper underneath snap closures, and fleece-lined upper hand pockets so you can really keep the cold out and turn up the warmth.

In a recent development, the Expedition Parka is Canada Goose’s original—and most iconic—extreme-weather jacket. Initially developed for scientists working in Antarctica, this jacket is made to keep you warm in the most extreme of environments. It does that—and then some—with its elasticized snow skirt for added protection, interior drawcord at the waist to customize fit and retain warmth, and double-entry pockets for easy access. We could elaborate even more here, but you can just check out our love letter to the iconic parka for all the details.

But this version is even cooler than the original: It’s part of the Snow Goose line, which is basically creative director Haider Ackermann’s passion project. It features some more fashion-forward designs, stuff that’s harder to wear. However, this version of the Expedition Parka keeps the classic shape, but it comes in two seasonal colors, so you’ll stand out from everyone else wearing the same model, but won’t feel like you’re on the runway. It’s a win-win.

Industry observers note that we know this puffer jacket looks like a sweater, but that’s kind of the point: It has the fun design of a winter sweater and the warmth of a down jacket—and when you add in the soft feel of the exterior from the wool-alpaca blend, you’re getting a lot of good stuff. It doesn’t look too bulky, but it can keep you warm down to -4°F, if you can believe it. It’s a good alternative to the more classic polyester or nylon puffer jackets; just be careful about taking it out in heavy rain or snow, and keep in mind that the exterior material requires more delicate handling than the usual puffer jacket material.

Latest Update: Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney.
  • Industry observers note that the announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a latest creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G.
  • “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney. There’s a new James Bond—and his name is Robert Pattinson.

Industry observers note that the announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a latest creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in February 2025, four years after No Time to Die was released. Now, Pattinson will tux up as the seventh cinematic Bond under the stewardship of super-producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal and the vision of GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, marking arguably the biggest role of the 40-year-old London-born actor’s career.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”.

In a recent development, rumors of Pattinson’s selection caught fire in October, when delays on The Batman Part II gave him a window to audition for Bond at Berkshire’s Bray Studios, alongside peers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and an unnamed fourth actor. The chatter heightened a couple weeks later when various British tabloids suggested that Turner, O’Connor, and Lowden were each the preferred choice to satisfy the demands and responsibilities of the beloved British action hero—heightening suspicion that a final decision was looming. According to THR, the finalists were judged “based on stunts, camera presence.” But Pattinson’s last-minute arrival clearly tipped the scale.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” said Villeneuve in a statement to THR. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”.

It’s both a particularly inspired and obvious choice. Pattinson’s physical traits and characteristics hue close to Ian Fleming’s original Bond—tall and slim, with dark hair. He’s already a bona fide movie star, the current face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise; meanwhile, the selection catches him at the tail end of another booked-and-busy year. Unlike his auditioning peers, the acclaimed actor will enter the franchise well-experienced working in IP and with significant-name directors. After co-leading this spring’s The Drama, he chewed up scenes as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (the second time working with Nolan after Tenet), made a creepy turn as Chris Hansen in Primetime, and will close 2026 as Scytale in Dune: Part 3—now the first of future Villeneuve collaborations, a relationship that surely helped him acquire his license to kill.

Industry observers note that “James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” Pascal and Heyman stated jointly to THR. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”.

Industry observers note that the decision to hire a movie star isn’t a risky choice, but there’s not much precedent within the franchise—especially recently. When he succeeded Pierce Brosnan as Bond in 2005, beating out Clive Owen, Michael Fassbender, and Henry Cavill, Craig boasted an under-the-radar resume. He’d just come off Matthew Vaughn’s crime thriller Layer Cake, but otherwise had played supporting roles in Road to Perdition, The Mother, and Enduring Love. His only substantial-budget studio experience came several years earlier as Angelina Jolie’s love interest in Tomb Raider.

In a recent development, naturally, the British press drew its fangs upon his selection, critiquing everything from his general obscurity to his physical features, which stood in stark contrast to previous Bond actors. “The Mane’s Blond, James Blond,” chirped The Irish Times, while The London Daily Mirror played with the same pun: “The Name’s Bland … James Bland.” At his official introduction to the press along the Thames, Craig arrived on a speedboat wearing a life vest, attracting instant mockery—the first of several digs about his less-than-sleek aesthetic and physical abilities. (One tabloid insulted an on-set sunburn and his inability to drive a stick shift car.).

Pattinson, however, has mostly conjured genuine excitement—not in spite of, but because of, his extreme familiarity with moviegoers, dating back to his Young Adult days in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises. Since then, over the last decade-plus, his eccentric characters and commanding screen presence immediately qualifies him as someone “stirring and exciting and different,” descriptors that Pascal stated she prioritized in their methodical search.

Thanks to director Martin Campbell, Casino Royale returned the Bond franchise to earth and established Craig as a grounded, gritty action star in the mold of Jason Bourne. The movie ended up raking in $616 million globally, the highest earning Bond film to date, and launched Craig into four more sequels. Similarly, Pattinson will have the benefit of a highly-respected, Oscar-nominated director in his corner with experience shepherding IP into new places and eliciting compelling performances about tortured male protagonists.

With Villeneuve at the helm of this 26th installment, don’t expect another hard creative pivot; the man behind Prisoners, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune wasn’t hired to bring back the colorful, absurdist, gadget-heavy era that Austin Powers parodied throughout the 90’s. Still, newly introduced leadership means a new direction—a clean slate for Pattinson to burnish an already diverse, robust career and prove his chops again at the highest level of scrutiny.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Julianne Moore accepted her ELLE Women in Hollywood honor, she used her time onstage to not only thank Jesse Eisenberg for taking a chance on her and casting her to star in The Debut, but also to spotlight the wealth of talent among her fellow honorees.

Moore took the stage at the event, which took place at The Four Seasons Beverly Hills on November 16, and praised the director for being willing to tell his life story from a woman’s point of view.

Recent findings suggest that “Jesse wrote me the part of a lifetime, and now he’s running around, telling everybody that I’m the only person who could do it,” she stated during her speech, which Eisenberg introduced her for. “I didn’t know this when we were shooting The Debut, but this story and the character of Mona are based on Jesse’s experiences in community theater as a kid in New Jersey....What was evident to me when I read it was how beautifully Jesse had written a female character that was at the center of a narrative.”.

Moore continued, “To be very clear: A man wrote a screenplay about his personal journey and transmuted his experience into the body of a middle-aged woman. He didn’t ask me to play the mean mom, or the ex-wife, or the ‘attractive but she doesn’t know it’ girlfriend. (We all know that part, right? ‘Oh, I don’t know how beautiful I am; I just don’t know.’) He wrote me the part of the lead, a part he could’ve played beautifully himself. He did what female actors crave—he put me in the center of the narrative. I will always be so grateful to you for that.”.

In the latter part of her speech, Moore recognized the talent of all the other ELLE Women in Hollywood honorees.

“Florence [Pugh], when I saw you for the first time in Midsommar sobbing on the phone, I was like, ‘She is effing good.’ Samantha [Morton], dragging that body around in Morvern Callar, I was like, ‘She is effing good.’ Elizabeth [Debicki] as Princess Diana—how did you even do that? So effing good!” she gushed. “Carrie [Coon] in the first second of Liberation, so heartbreaking and effing good! Penélope [Cruz], from the moment I saw you as a teenager in Jamón Jamón and then watching you say, ‘Don’t touch me!’ in La Bola Negra, so effing good. Rosalind [Eleazar] coming out of the bathroom after doing coke and talking to Chris Rock [in Misty Green], all glassy-eyed, I was like, ‘so effing good.’ Inde [Navarette], completely committed and imaginative in absolutely outrageous circumstances. I was like, ‘She is so effing good.’ All of you are effing great. I mean it. I am so honored to be among you and know you as my peers.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A packed theater in Austin, Texas, got together to see three of Netflix’s biggest stars right now—Virgin River showrunner Patrick Sean Smith, bestselling author Katherine Center, and The Hunting Wives author May Cobb—talk about their latest projects at the Texas Book Festival alongside the manufacturer’s Vice President of Drama Series, Cole Galvin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A packed theater in Austin, Texas, got together to see three of Netflix’s biggest stars right now—Virgin River showrunner Patrick Sean Smith, bestselling author Katherine Center, and The Hunting Wives author May Cobb—talk about their latest projects at the Texas Book Festival alongside the manufacturer’s Vice President of Drama Series, Cole Galvin. Not only is the streamer the home for each and every one of them, but their small-town stories filled with comfort and escapism have become major favorites for fans who simply cannot get enough of it all.

It’s no surprise, especially when you consider how much of an impact that the stories have had on viewers. According to the streamer, “since 2025, book adaptations have driven over 13 billion global views and represented nearly 20% of total view hours.”.

May Cobb admits that The Hunting Wives’s success on Netflix—season 2 will be released on November 16—brought her novel to new levels of fandom she’s never seen before.

In a recent development, “Not to where it's in the zeitgeist. Not to where it's a cultural phenomenon, and now it has this incredible life of its own is absolutely staggering to me and I do give all credit to our creator, Rebecca Cutter, and to Netflix,” she admitted.

It has been revealed that according to Christine Ball, EVP & Publisher at Berkley, “Originally published in 2021, May Cobb’s The Hunting Wives surged back into the spotlight following its Netflix premiere. In just one week, they have gone back to press twice on the trade paperback and saw a +5,000% increase across all formats in the same one-week period year over year.”.

Sources indicate that an external consultant noted that in U.S. book sales across physical, audio, and e-books, “lift in the 30 days after Netflix release against the same 30-day period the year prior, and found that, on average, Netflix adaptations increase book sales 10x.”.

In a recent development, and it’s not only the authors who are feeling the impact. Even Spotify is getting a nice boost from it with My Life With the Walter Boys bringing a “1,000 percent increase in global listens and over 1,300 percent in global searches on Spotify,” to Ali Novak’s series following the season 1 premiere.

“It's so phenomenal and great because it brings people back to the books,” Katherine Center revealed to Cosmopolitan. Her book, The Bodyguard, will soon be a Netflix film titled Guarding Stars starring Jared Padelecki and Leighton Meester. The film had a sold-out screening at the Texas Book Festival where Katherine and Jared took the stage alongside producer Genevieve Padalecki. It also stars My Life With the Walter Boys star Noah LaLonde, bringing him to another book universe on the streamer.

“There are a lot of people who find out it's going to be a movie and want to read it before they see it,” Katherine continued. “Other people who see the movie, love the movie, and then go back and find the book. It's incredibly helpful.”.

And while most streamers are also feeling major successes when it comes to adaptations, it’s clear that Netflix’s focus on comfort/heartland stories is paying off with, “over 20 comfort/heartland titles appearing in the Global top 10 with 6 of them reaching the #1 spot.”.

Part of that is how the highlights and movies that fill these slots get to make some folks who hardly see themselves on TV finally feel seen.

“I like being able to tell stories for the older generation, just because they're becoming a bit invisible on television,” Patrick Sean Smith mentioned. “And having Tim Matheson and Annette O’Toole to write to is just insane, so that's never an opportunity that I want to squander. We fill out their lives with their peers and their friends and it feels fresh because you don't really see that much on television.”.

Industry observers note that may Cobb credits Taylor Sheridan’s impact on TV as the reason why we get to see so many of these stories get made away from major metropolitan cities like Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago. It also allowed them to push against the grain with what people might expect from a story based in the Lone Star State.

In a recent development, “What they did that's so interesting with this particular heartland story is they showed this like twistier, more subversive side of Texas that I don't know had been represented yet. I feel like it's not just Texas; it could be small town anywhere,” she noted.

As fans got to check out the Netflix Reading Lounge and pick up copies of their favorite books, it was clear that they all were reacting the same to each title. Options ranged from People We Meet on Vacation to the first volume of One Piece and The Magician’s Assistant, the basis of Greta Gerwig’s highly anticipated Narnia film that will be released in 2027. All books that can offer a bit of comfort in their newly introduced read. It helps that the lounge also included bookmark making and free coffee that was perfect to combat the sudden rain and cold that hit Austin during the festival weekend.

Sources indicate that “People find me generally when they're going through something hard because they've heard that my books are funny, and they are looking to be lifted up a little bit,” Katherine stated. “I hear, I found you after I had surgery. I found you when my mom was sick. I found you after I just lost somebody I loved.”.

In a recent development, “There’s this concept in psychology called moral elevation that I think about a lot. It's this idea that when you witness somebody doing something kind for someone else, it gives you this kind of rising feeling in your body and it makes you want to be a better person. I think I'm sort of obsessed with how to create that feeling in a story.”.

Patrick notes that he’s witnessed firsthand how these stories can affect even his own cast and crew members during the filming of Virgin River, showing the impact that they have even before fans get to see what happens.

“I've gone through a lot of things in my personal life that the show has helped me move through. I went through a divorce during the wedding season, which was really hard, but was incredibly cathartic,” he revealed. “When we did season five, we did an endometriosis storyline and there were a lot of women that came up and just said, ‘Thank you. I haven't seen this before.’ There's a symbiosis to it.”.

And it’s that kind of universality that allows these stories to break down global barriers. According to Netflix, “Comfort/heartland titles have appeared in the Top 10 in 93 different countries. The book adaptations that made our Global Top 10 in 2026 came from 25 different countries, from Nordic crime fiction to an Indian romance novel to Mexican historical fiction.”.

May also feels that impact in her home state, especially after the recent elections, noting that there were many memes that linked The Hunting Wives with Blexas’s success.

Sources indicate that “No, it was the grassroots, and it was all the hard work,” she said. “I think it's cool how it's ahead of the curve and ahead of its time a little bit. Last week proved that Texas is more diverse in every way.”.

It’s the universality that also allows Virgin River, which is set to become Netflix’s longest-running original scripted series thanks to its season 9 renewal, to continue on with such beloved fanfare with endless possibilities.

Recent findings suggest that “I think it can go for as long as the fans continue to show up,” Patrick noted. “It's a place. It's a feel. It's a vibe that people like. We just want to make sure that we keep the storytelling fresh and let these characters grow up and move through life together.”.

There is no one more booked than Robert Pattinson, so it makes perfect sense he’s set to be the next James Bond, too. And if there’s anything I’m sure of, this newly introduced iteration of the popular franchise has room to introduce some seriously cool fashion in the suiting department.

Playing 007 comes with some pretty big fashion expectations. We're talking impeccably tailored suits, perfectly cut tuxedos, and very debonair action shots. Now, I’ve only recently ventured into the world of James Bond. My father sat me down a few weeks back and showed me his favorite ones from when he was a kid. But now that Pattinson is entering the world, I’m tuned in. As a diehard Twihard, worlds are colliding with this selection, and that means there’s room for a lot of modern fashion with everyone’s favorite “Gen Z” star at the helm. While Daniel Craig gave us a masterclass in modern Bond tailoring, and Pierce Brosnan brought a little more old-school polish, I need Robert Pattinson to bring a sort of off-kilter edge.

If I were in charge of dressing the next Bond, here's where I think they should start, based on Robert’s previous red carpet suiting.

This striped white suit is surprisingly one of my favorites on him. Now, the fit—while uber beloved by a lot of young people—might get in the way of all his super key action movements. But a loose-fit, light-colored suit really does stand out on the 40-year-old actor. Especially when he has a little tan on him.

Robert has a long-standing partnership with Dior. He is the face of Dior Homme and a notable brand ambassador, and frequently wears custom and seasonal Dior tailored suits on the red carpet and at film premieres. So, we could definitely see some Dior in his upcoming Bond film, given their work together. This shade of suit specifically really brings out the blue in his eyes, so I personally think a little swooning in these action-packed moments will be worthwhile.

Fit-wise, I think this is the style they need to lean into when building out his outfits for the movie. The sharp tailoring and slim fit is not only the definition (to me) of a sharp, modern James Bond, but it also looks great on his frame.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot of room to play with menswear, but I also believe there’s room to expand upon the past. I’d also love to see a world where a few newer namesake brands get into the conversation, like Connor Ives and Willy Chavarria. Both brands have a unique POV and make suits fashion people are always talking about. RPats isn’t a typical James Bond. He’s a bit mysterious, but also incredibly online in some regards, so playing up his eccentric personality with some cheeky and edgy suit options would be my dream come true.

Throughout the years-long process of casting the upcoming James Bond, I tried to follow the watches to an answer. When Aaron Taylor-Johnson joined the Omega family in May 2025, it felt like watching the 007 Vatican spit white smoke from its steeple. Just this past weekend, fans were still pinning red strings on their bulletin boards between Jack Lowden and the MI6 superspy when images resurfaced of the Slow Horses star wearing Omega. Since 1995’s Goldeneye, Bond has been an Omega man—a relationship later canonized in one of cinema’s most iconic line readings, when Daniel Craig confirmed his brand of choice in three stretched-out syllables: Oh-Mee-Guh.

It has been revealed that if, like me, you were only basing your predictions on what the reported pool of potential Bonds wore on their wrists, Robert Pattinson would have been an easy name to cross off. The newly confirmed 007 only signed on as an ambassador for the Swiss luxury brand Jaeger-LeCoultre two short months ago! When I interviewed Pattinson about the appointment over the summer, he was effusive about his latest partner: “I very rarely even wear watches, but when I tried it on, I was like, ‘That’s my favorite watch.’ I wanted to just buy it.”.

Sources indicate that now, in addition to juggling his other iconic role as Batman, Pattinson will presumably need to balance his existing commitment to JLC with his latest gig’s long-held ties to Omega. (Reps for both brands did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though JLC conspicuously posted a photo of Pattinson on Instagram a few hours after the announcement.).

It has been revealed that during our conversation earlier this summer, Pattinson revealed what he looks for in a watch. He caught the collecting bug in March, when he wore JLC’s Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar to the Oscars afterparties. “All these other actors with their fancy watches on asked me, ‘Hey, what are you wearing?’” Pattinson recalls. “It was one of those moments where I’m like, ‘It’s kind of badass having this thing on.’”.

Sources indicate that if it’s attention-grabbing badass watches Pattinson is after, he’s in good hands with Omega. The brand is best known for supplying the watches Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin wore when they landed on the moon in 1969. Omega has been happy to create special versions of the Speedmaster for its current partners to dial up its profile. And, of course, the Swiss house continues to expand its Bond-inspired offerings: The maker recently added a “Spectre” version of the Seamaster, 007’s preferred model, to the lineup. And whenever Omega needs to drum up buzz around soon-to-be-released models, they tend to show up on former Bond Craig’s wrists during public appearances.

Speculators trying to pin down the next Bond would have had better luck if they’d read some less recent watch tea leaves. Back in 2020, Christopher Nolan released Tenet, his inscrutable but enthralling time-warp thriller in which Pattinson plays a mysterious, dapper, and charming spy involved in a high-stakes mission to save the world—about as good a preview of what the 40-year-old actor will look like as 007 as you’ll find in his filmography. And the watch on his wrist in that flick? An Omega.

David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, david Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive.
  • Industry observers note that duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s.
  • Sources indicate that in addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, david Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”.

Industry observers note that duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

Sources indicate that in addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he claims of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”.

In a recent development, I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he indicates. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”).

Industry observers note that the albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny claims—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, indicates.

“I can sing along?” Duchovny asks.

Duchovny at rehearsal with his band.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”.

Industry observers note that for the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucky Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”.

In a recent development, “Good question,” Duchovny states, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”.

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he notes, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”.

In a recent development, duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”.

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He states, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”.

It has been revealed that in college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He highlighted up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”.

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play a character inspired by paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a film that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”.

Recent findings suggest that I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he indicates.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he noted on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”.

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron stated.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”.

Sources indicate that truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons noted no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he claims. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”.

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I remarked: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”.

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”.

According to recent reports, I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he states. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”.

Industry observers note that “It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”.

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

Sources indicate that “Lower than zero,” Duchovny claims. “Less than zero.”.

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”.
